reviewBoundary: Six complete original senior five-of-seven plus ten-gap grammar practices, two per level. Each grammar has seven given-word and three single-word positions; shared candidates shuffled with exact-key assertions. Same-author cohesion/form/variant review only, no independent calibration.

units.alignmentNote: Old sources are level/family drafting references only. Final National I structure: complete five-gap seven-option insertion plus complete ten-gap grammar passage.

materials.title: A. Choosing a poem and making a clay cup
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
Finding a poem you enjoy need not begin with deciding whether you understand poetry as a whole. A short encounter with one particular poem can be enough. The aim is to notice a response worth exploring, not to pass an invisible entrance test.

Start with something you can read more than once without rushing. ____1____ The second reading may reveal a sound or image you missed while simply finding your way through the lines.

Try reading aloud, quietly if necessary. ____2____ A line that looked ordinary on the page may gather force through repetition, rhythm or an unexpected pause.

Do not treat every unfamiliar reference as an immediate barrier. Mark what puzzles you and continue to the end. ____3____ Sometimes the surrounding poem supplies enough context to begin; sometimes a brief later check will help.

Notice what stays with you. It may be an image rather than a message you can paraphrase. ____4____ You can ask how the words create that effect before deciding what the poem means overall.

Finally, allow yourself a preference. ____5____ Reading another poem can be a sensible next step. Enjoyment and careful attention can develop together without requiring admiration for every piece you meet.
candidates: A. The poet may have published the work in a collection years earlier.
B. Hearing the language adds another way to encounter its movement.
C. Disliking one poem does not prevent you from enjoying another.
D. A manageable length leaves room for returning to the same words.
E. You can return to the reference after seeing where it leads.
F. A library may place poetry on shelves beside plays.
G. That lingering detail is a useful starting point for closer reading.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 1.
questions.explanation: D explains why manageable length helps repeated reading. B sound/E reference/G remembered effect/C preference fit later; A/F publication or shelving change topic.

questions.explanation: B connects aloud reading to sound/rhythm/pause. Other choices do not develop hearing the language.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 3.
questions.explanation: E refers to marked puzzling reference and prepares later context/check. D length/B sound/G lingering image/C preference are other moves.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 4.
questions.explanation: G refers to the image that remains and introduces examining its effect. Other options do not connect remembered detail with close reading.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 5.
questions.explanation: C validates a particular dislike and leads to trying another poem. A publication/F shelves do not explain preference; the four remaining options concern reading methods.

materials.title: B. Choosing a poem and making a clay cup
materials.instruction: Fill each gap with one appropriate word or the correct form of the word in brackets.
materials.text:
Our class visited a pottery studio for a supervised workshop. I ____1____ (expect) to make a perfect cup, although I had never shaped clay before. The instructor gave us a small piece and asked us to feel how it changed under our hands.

Several ____2____ (example) stood on a shelf. They showed different shapes, but we were not required to copy one exactly. The instructor reminded us that a cup needed a stable base as well ____3____ an attractive outline.

I began by pressing too hard. The wall became thin in one place, and ____4____ (I) first shape leaned to the side. Rather than hide the problem with decoration, I asked how to make the thickness more even.

The instructor showed me how to support the outside while pressing gently inside. She asked me ____5____ (work) slowly and check the result after each small movement. A rushed repair could create another weak area.

We left space ____6____ the handle to be attached later. The workshop used a particular process for drying and firing, which staff would complete after we left. A finished shape was not yet a ready-to-use drinking cup.

My second attempt was ____7____ (good) than the first. I moved my fingers ____8____ (careful) and paid attention to the base. The piece ____9____ (label) before being placed with the others for the next stage.

I would collect it after the studio's checks were complete. It was ____10____ useful lesson in how a visible object can pass through several unfinished stages. What I carried home that afternoon was a photograph and a clearer idea of the work still ahead.

materials.title: A. Looking at leaves and arranging a visit
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
A familiar plant can become surprisingly difficult to describe once you stop relying on its name. Looking carefully at a leaf offers a practical starting point. You need not identify every species to make an observation more precise.

Begin with the whole outline. Is it long, rounded or divided into sections? ____1____ A simple sketch can preserve a relationship that a general word such as green leaves unclear.

Then examine the edge. A smooth border differs from one with regular teeth or deeper cuts. ____2____ Recording that feature can help later comparison even when the plant's name remains uncertain.

Look at arrangement as well as individual shape. Leaves may meet a stem in different patterns. ____3____ One detached leaf cannot show every feature of the plant from which it came.

Keep the circumstances of the observation. Note the place and date, and avoid damaging plants or entering restricted areas to obtain a specimen. ____4____ A view recorded responsibly is more useful than a supposed identification with no clear basis.

Finally, distinguish observation from identification. ____5____ A guide or expert may help connect the recorded features with a name. Until then, a careful description can remain valuable without pretending the question has been settled.
candidates: A. A book cover may use a leaf as a decorative symbol.
B. Such differences can be visible without specialised equipment.
C. A photograph and notes may be enough for the purpose.
D. The relation between parts matters as much as a quick colour label.
E. Observe how several leaves connect, not only one leaf in isolation.
F. Describing what you see is not the same as establishing a species.
G. Some gardens sell plants during the spring.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 1.
questions.explanation: D elaborates outline/parts and prepares sketch versus vague colour. B edge/E stem/C recording/F identification belong later; G/A unrelated.

questions.explanation: B refers to visible edge differences and supports recording them. Other choices do not develop this readily observed feature.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 3.
questions.explanation: E adds stem arrangement to individual shape, developed by detached-leaf limit. D outline/B edge/C records/F naming are separate points.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 4.
questions.explanation: C offers non-damaging documentation after responsible-observation rules. Other options do not provide that method.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 5.
questions.explanation: F explicitly separates observed description from species identification, preparing guide/expert step. G/A do not address evidentiary distinction.

materials.title: B. Looking at leaves and arranging a visit
materials.instruction: Fill each gap with one appropriate word or the correct form of the word in brackets.
materials.text:
Our class arranged a visit to a local history room. Before booking, the teacher asked us ____1____ (check) the opening times and the conditions for groups. The room was small, so a large class could not assume it would be admitted without discussion.

We wrote several ____2____ (question) for the organiser. One concerned the number of visitors; another asked whether everyone could enter ____3____ the same time. The reply suggested dividing the class into two groups with a short changeover.

A student ____4____ list contained all the names helped organise the groups. We did not publish private contact information on the noticeboard. The teacher kept the details needed for the visit separately.

After ____5____ (receive) confirmation, we prepared our questions about the objects. We had seen photographs, but the visit would also let us ask about materials, scale and the reasons for particular display choices.

The organiser explained the handling rules ____6____ (clear). Some replicas could be touched, while originals remained protected. Being invited into the room did not give us permission to handle every object.

Our first group ____7____ (welcome) at ten. The second waited with a teacher in an agreed space nearby. The short gap between groups was used for ____8____ (reset) the room rather than treated as spare time for additional visitors.

We returned to school with ____9____ (we) notes and several new questions. It had been ____10____ interesting visit partly because we could connect the visible displays with the practical decisions that made the visit possible. A booking email had been the start of that work, not a complete description of it.

materials.title: A. Quoting a translation and reading a letter
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
Quoting a translated passage involves more than copying words from a page. A reader may need to know both the original work and the particular translation that supplied the wording. Those are connected references, but they do not identify the same contribution.

Begin by naming the translation actually used. ____1____ Two versions can differ in phrasing, rhythm and explanatory choices even when they translate the same original sentence.

Preserve enough surrounding context to keep the quotation fair. ____2____ A sentence expressing a character's doubt should not become evidence of the book's confident conclusion merely because its qualifying lines have disappeared.

If you alter a quotation for a specific purpose, explain the intervention. ____3____ Readers should be able to distinguish the published wording from a change you introduced.

Be cautious about arguments that depend on one translated word alone. ____4____ The issue may concern a translator's choice, the original expression or a relation between them that requires further examination.

Finally, distinguish access from permission. ____5____ A text available online still has conditions governing reuse. Accurate reference helps identify a source; it does not by itself settle every question about how that source may be reproduced.
candidates: A. Check whether the same claim survives comparison with other relevant evidence.
B. The translator and edition help identify the words a reader will find.
C. A printed edition may use a different cover design in another country.
D. That may include clearly marking an omission or your own added explanation.
E. Selection can change a passage’s apparent force without changing its spelling.
F. Some books appear in more than one physical size.
G. Being able to obtain a passage does not automatically authorise every use.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 1.
questions.explanation: B identifies translator/edition as actual wording source. E selection/D intervention/A evidence/G permission fit later; C/F physical design do not identify phrasing.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 2.
questions.explanation: E explains context selection changing force, illustrated by doubt/conclusion example. Others do not address omitted qualifying context.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 3.
questions.explanation: D specifies interventions after alteration and prepares published-versus-added distinction. Other choices do not explain editorial changes.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 4.
questions.explanation: A proposes comparison for a single-word argument, developed by distinguishing source/translation relationship. B identification/E context/D edits/G rights concern other checks.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 5.
questions.explanation: G separates availability from permission and leads to reuse conditions. C/F format and the four remaining source-interpretation options do not settle rights.

materials.title: B. Quoting a translation and reading a letter
materials.instruction: Fill each gap with one appropriate word or the correct form of the word in brackets.
materials.text:
A letter in our fictional history exercise ____1____ (write) during a journey, but its date was partly damaged. The page described a delayed train and a meeting the writer hoped to reach. We were asked to state what could be known without filling every gap by guesswork.

Several ____2____ (detail) were legible. The station name survived, as did a reference to a Monday departure. Those clues narrowed the possibilities, but they did not identify a unique date ____3____ themselves.

Our teacher asked us ____4____ (compare) the letter with a timetable from the same period. The timetable showed planned services, not a complete record of trains that actually ran. A reported delay could not be disproved merely because no delay appeared in the printed schedule.

After ____5____ (examine) both documents, we wrote a short account. It distinguished the writer's statement from our interpretation. The pupil ____6____ had transcribed the damaged line also marked where a reading remained uncertain.

The first draft sounded more ____7____ (confidence) than our evidence justified. We revised it ____8____ (careful), replacing a claim of exact arrival time with a narrower description of what the letter said.

Our final notes ____9____ (keep) beside copies of the two sources. The original exercise materials remained intact. It was ____10____ useful demonstration of how a clear account can include uncertainty without becoming empty. We had not discovered every answer, but we could explain both our conclusion and the limits that shaped it.

materials.title: A. Reading a story aloud and making bookmarks
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
Reading a story aloud to a group differs from reading it silently to yourself. The listeners cannot choose their own pace or look back whenever they wish. A few practical choices can help them follow without turning every sentence into a performance trick.

Read the whole story before the session. ____1____ Knowing what comes later helps you decide which early details need to be clear without revealing the ending.

Choose a pace that leaves room for listeners to imagine the scene. ____2____ A short pause after a surprising event can give them time to connect it with what came before.

Make different speakers distinguishable, but do not assume each needs an elaborate accent. ____3____ Small changes are often easier to maintain consistently across a complete story.

Watch the group without treating every movement as a sign of boredom. A listener may look down while concentrating. ____4____ If you need to check understanding, ask a relevant question rather than demanding that everyone sit in exactly the same way.

At the end, leave space for a response. ____5____ Their question or remembered image can show what the story has made available, even if it differs from the detail you expected them to notice.
candidates: A. A book may be available in several cover designs.
B. A first encounter is not the best time to discover a change in direction.
C. Attention does not always have one visible posture.
D. Speed that feels fluent to you may be too quick for someone hearing it once.
E. Some authors write for more than one age group.
F. Let the listeners speak before supplying your own summary.
G. A slight shift in tone or rhythm may be enough.

materials.text:
Our class ____1____ (make) bookmarks for the school book fair last week. Each one needed to be strong enough to use, but thin enough not to damage a page. We tested a spare strip of card before choosing the material.

There were several ____2____ (design) on the board. Some used long messages, while others had only a small drawing. We wanted readers to enjoy them without assuming that every bookmark needed the same style.

The teacher asked us ____3____ (write) a name on the back of each finished piece. That would help return it ____4____ its maker if it fell from a book before the fair. A decorative front alone would not identify every pupil.

I drew a bird and added two lines from a poem I had written myself. ____5____ (I) friend chose a simple pattern of circles. We checked spelling and left enough space around the edge so the words would remain clear after trimming.

The first strips ____6____ (cut) by the teacher using the approved equipment. We handled only the parts appropriate for us. Making many copies did not require everyone to use every tool.

After ____7____ (finish), we placed the bookmarks in paper sleeves. I described my design ____8____ (careful) on a small display card, saying why I had chosen the bird rather than claiming it would suit every reader.

At the fair, a visitor chose my friend's circles. Another liked the poem. Their different preferences gave us something to discuss. It was ____9____ useful reminder that a shared practical task can leave room ____10____ personal choices.

materials.title: A. Lines of equal height and a route description
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
A contour map can represent a three-dimensional landscape on a flat page. Its lines do not show paths that someone has built. Each contour connects points at the same elevation under the map's stated reference system.

Begin with the contour interval. ____1____ Without knowing that vertical step, the spacing between lines cannot be interpreted properly.

Look at how closely neighbouring lines lie. On a map with a consistent interval, tightly packed contours indicate a steeper change across the horizontal distance. ____2____ The relationship concerns slope, not the thickness of the ink.

Notice labels as well as patterns. A series of nested shapes may show rising or falling ground, depending on the values and symbols provided. ____3____ A familiar-looking pattern is not enough if its direction has been assumed rather than read.

Remember that the map is a representation at a chosen scale. ____4____ A small feature may be simplified or absent without implying that the real ground is perfectly smooth.

Finally, connect map reading with appropriate judgement about a journey. ____5____ Understanding contours can inform a question about terrain, but it is not a substitute for the skills, permissions and current information required in a particular place.
candidates: A. Its level of detail cannot include every small surface variation.
B. A map alone does not guarantee that a route is open or suitable.
C. Wider spacing represents the same vertical change spread over more ground.
D. A town name can change while a hill keeps its shape.
E. The interval states the elevation difference between adjacent contour levels.
F. The paper may have been printed in several colours.
G. Read the numbers before deciding which way the land rises.

Our walking club prepared a written description of a short public route. We ____1____ (visit) it with the teacher before writing the final version, because a path shown on an older map might not match current conditions.

Several ____2____ (change) were needed. A gate had been moved, and a sign that once stood beside the bridge was no longer there. We recorded the new landmarks rather than copy instructions that had become misleading.

The pupil ____3____ notebook held our draft read each stage aloud. Another followed the words while looking at the ground ahead. This helped reveal which instruction depended on knowledge the writer had forgotten to include.

The teacher asked us ____4____ (distinguish) a landmark from an optional detail. A red door might be noticeable today, but its colour could change. A more stable feature might make the direction easier to follow in future.

After ____5____ (compare) alternatives, we revised the turning point. The new sentence was ____6____ (clear) than the original because it named both the bridge and the direction immediately after it.

We explained the route ____7____ (careful), including its limits. Our short walk did not qualify us to promise that the path would always be open or suitable for every visitor. The date of our check remained ____8____ the page.

The final description ____9____ (keep) with the map we had used. It was ____10____ useful record of a particular visit, ready for another responsible check when circumstances changed.

materials.title: A. A time capsule and a catalogue entry
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
A time capsule is designed for an unknown future audience. That makes selection both appealing and difficult. An ordinary object may be obvious to its maker while leaving a later reader unsure what it was for or why it mattered.

Give each item enough context. ____1____ A label naming its use and the circumstances of selection can preserve more than an unexplained object alone.

Avoid treating the contributors as a complete sample of their time. ____2____ Their choices may reflect one class, workplace or neighbourhood rather than a whole generation.

Distinguish a present description from a prediction. ____3____ A note about how people use a device now is a different claim from a confident statement about what everyone will use in fifty years.

Consider the relationship between intention and survival. Materials and storage conditions can affect what remains readable. ____4____ Appropriate expert advice is more useful than assuming that a sealed box makes every object permanent.

Finally, record the project outside the container too. ____5____ A future opening is more likely to be understood if someone can discover when the capsule was made, what agreement governed it and where its supporting record can be found.
candidates: A. Some contributors may decorate their labels by hand.
B. State who participated and whose experiences may be missing.
C. Mark which kind of statement the writer is making.
D. Familiarity now does not guarantee intelligibility later.
E. An item that cannot be located may never meet its intended readers.
F. A photograph can be printed in several sizes.
G. The wish to preserve something is not itself a preservation method.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 1.
questions.explanation: D connects familiar present object with future intelligibility and need for context. Other options address sampling/claims/storage/location or decoration.

materials.title: B. A time capsule and a catalogue entry
materials.instruction: Fill each gap with one appropriate word or the correct form of the word in brackets.
materials.text:
For a school exhibition, we ____1____ (create) catalogue entries for several ordinary objects. One was an old lunchbox, another a bus ticket and a third a small painted stone. Their importance depended partly on the stories attached to them.

The teacher asked us ____2____ (separate) information written on an object from information supplied by its owner. A date printed on a ticket was not the same kind of evidence ____3____ a later memory about the journey.

Several ____4____ (question) followed. Had a handwritten name been added when the lunchbox was new? Did the painted stone come from the place its owner remembered? We could record an account without presenting every detail as independently confirmed.

The pupil ____5____ had taken the photographs checked that each image matched the correct entry. A clear caption on the wrong object would still mislead. We numbered the temporary display cards to keep the relationship visible.

After ____6____ (review) the drafts, we removed one unsupported claim. The revised entry was less definite but more ____7____ (accuracy) about the state of our knowledge. It explained who had supplied the information and which detail remained uncertain.

We labelled ____8____ (we) sources carefully. The entries ____9____ (preserve) beside the exhibition photographs so another class could inspect the record later. It was ____10____ useful exercise in making a description both readable and accountable, without pretending that every everyday object arrived with a complete history.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 1 with the correct form of create.
questions.explanation: Created/had created fit past catalogue preparation. Base/-ing do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 2 with the correct form of separate.
questions.explanation: Asked us takes to separate. Other listed forms do not fit directly.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 3 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: The same kind as forms comparison of evidential kinds. Than/to do not complete same ... as.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 4 with the correct form of question.
questions.explanation: Several requires plural questions. Singular/process noun do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 5 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Pupil as subject antecedent takes who/that. Which normally nonhuman and where not subject.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 6 with the correct form of review.
questions.explanation: After reviewing/having reviewed fit prior draft inspection. Other listed forms do not fit directly.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 7 with the correct form of accuracy.
questions.explanation: More accurate after was requires adjective. Noun/adverb do not fit linking complement.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 8 with the correct form of we.
questions.explanation: Our determines sources. Personal/independent possessive forms do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 9 with the correct form of preserve.
questions.explanation: Plural entries receive preservation. Bare participle lacks auxiliary and was disagrees.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 10 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Useful starts consonant /j/, so a. Other article readings remain reviewable.
